title: Frontend SEO and Structured Data
summary: Search engines need to understand what a page is about and whether it can be indexed.

subtopics.title: Page title
subtopics.explanation: A page title names a page in browser tabs, bookmarks, and search results. Make it specific and put the main subject early. It is like labeling each folder so people can tell them apart. Repeating the same title across a site makes pages harder to distinguish. For example, a unique title helps distinguish two articles about similar subjects. In a real page, write a title that distinguishes a product detail page from the product category.

subtopics.title: Description and headings
subtopics.explanation: A description summarizes what a page offers, while headings create a readable outline. These details should match what visitors can actually find. It is like writing an accurate catalog entry and chapter labels. Search engines may choose other text for a preview, so do not promise a guaranteed snippet. For example, a heading outline should describe sections that are visibly present on the page. In a real page, use headings that describe visible article sections in order.

subtopics.title: Crawlable links
subtopics.explanation: Crawlers discover pages through links and sitemaps. Important routes need stable addresses and links that can be followed. It is like creating connected paths through a library. Client navigation should still deliver useful page content and direct URLs should work. For example, a sitemap can help crawlers discover stable routes but does not guarantee indexing. In a real page, link important routes from ordinary navigable pages so crawlers can discover them.

subtopics.title: Structured data
subtopics.explanation: Structured data gives machines a standard description of a page entity, such as an article or product. JSON-LD is a common format. It is like adding a catalog card with labeled fields. The data must match visible content and does not guarantee enhanced search results. For example, a product JSON-LD block should match its visible name and price. In a real page, ensure a JSON-LD price matches the price shown to visitors.

subtopics.title: Indexing controls
subtopics.explanation: Robots directives can ask search engines not to index a page. Use them carefully for duplicate or temporary content. They are not access controls. It is like putting a “do not list” note on a public door; private content still needs server-side authorization. For example, use authorization rather than robots metadata to protect private account content. In a real page, protect private dashboards with authentication even when they are marked noindex.

foundations.overview: Search engine optimization helps people and crawlers understand and find useful pages. Clear titles, descriptive headings, crawlable links, and accurate metadata support that goal. Structured data can label page information for machines, but it does not guarantee a special search result. Think of SEO like a clear library catalog: it helps people locate books but does not make a poor book useful.
foundations.whyItMatters: Search metadata is useful only when it reflects accessible, current page content. Crawlability and authorization solve different problems and should be designed separately.
foundations.browserPerspective: Framework metadata becomes document head elements that browsers and crawlers can read.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Review each important route’s title, description, canonical address, and rendered content.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear previews help people find the right page and set accurate expectations.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Use a metadata convention so pages do not accidentally share titles or descriptions.
foundations.performanceImpact: Server rendering or static output can make important content easier to discover.
commonUseCases: Launch a content site with clear titles and page outlines.
Describe an article or product using accurate structured data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Structured data guarantees a rich search result
commonMisconceptions.reality: Search engines decide when and whether to show enhanced results.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A robots directive protects private content
commonMisconceptions.reality: It guides crawlers; server authorization must protect private data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Structured data guarantees a rich search result.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Search engines decide eligibility and presentation; markup must be valid and match page content.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A noindex directive hides a page from unauthorized visitors.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Indexing directives affect crawlers, not access; enforce privacy on the server.

keyTakeaways: A page title names a page in browser tabs, bookmarks, and search results.
A description summarizes what a page offers, while headings create a readable outline.
Crawlers discover pages through links and sitemaps.
Structured data gives machines a standard description of a page entity, such as an article or product.
Robots directives can ask search engines not to index a page.
